name: Aaron Gupta

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for your time, Aaron. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or political parties, and we don't sell anything. Everything you tell me is confidential. Could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at a kitchen cabinet factory off the bypass, about a hundred and twenty people. I run the edge-bander, which glues a thin strip onto the raw edge of each board so the cupboard doors look finished, and some days I help on the panel saw. I'm checking the glue temperature, feeding boards in the right way round, trimming and stacking, and making sure the colours match the order sheet, because a white edge on an oak door gets sent straight back. Two years in and I'm still the one who gets the trim settings wrong on the thick boards.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I worked in my father's corner shop from when I was sixteen, and I ran it for the last ten years after he got ill. The supermarket opened a small store across the road and we couldn't compete, so at 41 I closed it. It hurt, but you can't make people buy from you. The factory gave me a start, and I'm grateful, even if I'm the oldest junior on the floor.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a useful tool, but people got excited about nothing. Work still needs doing, and somebody still needs to do it. I'd say that at the mandir on Sunday, where the uncles love to argue about this stuff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I keep learning my trade, slowly, and keep my family steady. Anita's bookkeeping carries on, my job carries on. Good.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as now. Learn the panel saw properly, ask Terry, the supervisor, to put me forward for the CNC router training. We have about three months saved, and I'd keep adding to it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. I've had enough upheaval with the shop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you use any AI tools at the moment?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now and then. Arjun showed me how to ask it things, and I used it to write a complaint about our energy bill. It's handy, but I check what it says.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you want from the next few years in that world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: To get from junior to properly skilled. And to see Arjun into a good apprenticeship. That's what I want most.

S0.say: It's a useful tool, but people got excited about nothing, because work still needs doing by somebody. He'd say it at the temple on Sunday, where the older men love to argue about this.
S0.think: He keeps learning his trade slowly and keeps the family steady, with his wife's bookkeeping and his job both carrying on. That suits him.
S0.do: Learns the panel saw properly and asks his supervisor to put him forward for CNC router training. Keeps adding to the roughly three months of savings.
S0.feel: Calm, after enough upheaval with the shop.
S0.quote: I've had enough upheaval with the shop.
S0.fieldNote: Aaron's life has been shaped by losing his father's shop to a supermarket, and he values stability above all. He uses AI occasionally but checks its answers. His main hopes are about skill and his son's apprenticeship.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say companies have every right to bring in new machines, that's business. But they should train the people they have, and the government should back apprenticeships, not just benefits. That's how you keep families working.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'm worried about two things at once. The edge-bander already has a robot version, and a big firm down south uses it. And the bookkeeping is exactly what AI does well, so Anita's clients might not need her.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Terry for the CNC training straight away, because that's the machine that stays. We'd put another fifty a month aside and stop the takeaway on Saturdays. And I'd use the AI more once I saw it working for others, like the men on the CNC who already use it for programs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Two wages, both at risk, is a lot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned Anita's bookkeeping. How would this picture affect her?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She's already noticed. Two of her small clients started using an app to do their own books. She'd have to offer something the app can't, like sitting with them and explaining it. Or she'd need another job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd wait until it's proven. What would count as proven?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: When the lads on the CNC are using it every day and it's not breaking things. When Terry says it's fine. Then I'd learn it, properly, with someone showing me.

S1.say: Companies have every right to bring in new machines, but they should train their people and the government should back apprenticeships, not just benefits. That's how families keep working.
S1.think: He's worried about two things at once: a robot edge-bander already exists, and his wife's bookkeeping is exactly what AI does well. Both household incomes are exposed.
S1.do: Asks his supervisor for CNC training straight away, saves another fifty a month and drops the Saturday takeaway. Starts using AI more once he sees colleagues on the CNC using it successfully.
S1.feel: Anxious, because two wages are at risk at once.
S1.quote: Two wages, both at risk, is a lot.
S1.fieldNote: Aaron's worry comes from his household, not just his own job, because his wife's bookkeeping clients are already drifting to apps. He supports the company's right to automate while asking for training and apprenticeships. He would learn new tools once colleagues have proven them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is too fast, and families will suffer. I'd want the government to help businesses keep people on rather than hand out money. I'd say it at the mandir and to anyone who'd listen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, I'd lose my job, and so would Anita, probably within a year. We'd have a mortgage and two children and no wages. I've been through a shop closing, so I know how fast money goes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd cut everything back, holidays, the car, the extras. I'd ask my brother and Anita's family if they could help, and we'd look at taking in a lodger. I'd start doing small jobs on the side, fitting kitchens or flatpack, while people still want a person.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. Like the week the supermarket opened across the road.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With two years, what would you do in the first month?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sit with Anita and do the sums, like we did with the shop. Ring the bank early. And ask my uncle, who has a property, if he'd let us pay less rent if we had to sell up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Arjun, who's looking at apprenticeships?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That I don't know what to tell him, which is hard for a father. I'd say learn something with your hands, but even that might not be safe. I'd tell him to stay close to family, because that's the only thing that doesn't change.

S2.say: This is too fast and families will suffer. He'd want the government to help businesses keep people on rather than hand out money, and he'd say it at the temple and to anyone.
S2.think: He'd lose his job, and his wife likely within a year, leaving a mortgage and two children with no wages. Having closed a shop, he knows how fast money goes.
S2.do: Cuts holidays, car costs and extras, and asks his brother and his wife's family for help, considering a lodger. Starts small jobs fitting kitchens and flatpack furniture on the side, and rings the bank early.
S2.feel: Alarmed, like the week the supermarket opened across the road.
S2.quote: That I don't know what to tell him, which is hard for a father.
S2.fieldNote: The fast picture brings back his memory of the shop closing, and his response draws on family networks. He would start side work fitting kitchens, using his factory knowledge. His advice to his son is uncertain, falling back on family as the only constant.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time to prepare, so families should prepare. Companies should train their people for whatever's left. And apprenticeships, always apprenticeships.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years gives me time to learn the CNC and earn better for a while, and for Anita to find something else. But at 48, the same thing happens. I'd be more ready.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: CNC training in the first year, then start fitting kitchens at weekends to build a side business. We'd save hard, maybe two hundred a month. Anita would retrain, maybe as a teaching assistant, and I'd use the AI to help with quotes and costings, once I'd seen others do it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but better than the fast one. I'd have a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do the extra three years change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Time to build the fitting work properly, with a van and a name, not just a few jobs for cash. And time for Arjun to get through an apprenticeship.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still push for the CNC training?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, for a couple of years, because the pay's better. And because knowing how the cabinets are made helps me fit them. But I'd know it's not forever.

S3.say: There's time to prepare, so families should prepare and companies should train their people for whatever's left. Apprenticeships, always apprenticeships.
S3.think: Five years gives him time to learn the CNC and earn better, and for his wife to find something else. At 48 the same thing happens, but he'd be more ready.
S3.do: Takes CNC training in year one and starts fitting kitchens at weekends as a side business. Saves about two hundred a month and uses AI for quotes and costings once others have proven it.
S3.feel: Anxious, but better than the fast picture because he has a plan.
S3.quote: Time to build the fitting work properly, with a van and a name, not just a few jobs for cash.
S3.fieldNote: Aaron's shopkeeping past comes back as he plans a small fitting business with a van and a name. His factory knowledge feeds directly into that plan. His wife's retraining is part of a joint household strategy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough to do it the right way, with apprenticeships, training and families helping each other. No need to panic or wait for handouts. I'd say that to anyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years is a good stretch. I could learn the CNC, build the fitting business, and see both children into apprenticeships or college. At 53, I'd want to be my own boss again, like at the shop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: CNC training, then a fitting business on the side by year three. Save steadily, and maybe invest in a van and tools once the work's coming in. And make sure Arjun gets a good apprenticeship and Meera stays in school.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but more hopeful. Like opening a new shop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With ten years, what would you hold off on, if anything?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Taking on debt for the business too early. I've been burned before. I'd only buy the van when the work was steady.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where do you see yourself in 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Running a small fitting firm, maybe with Arjun. A father and son business, like my dad and me. If people still want a person in their house, that's where I'd be.

S4.say: Ten years is enough to do it the right way, with apprenticeships, training and families helping each other. There's no need to panic or wait for handouts.
S4.think: Ten years is enough to learn the CNC, build a fitting business and see both children into apprenticeships or college. At 53 he'd want to be his own boss again, like at the shop.
S4.do: Takes CNC training, then builds a side fitting business by year three. Saves steadily, invests in a van and tools only once work is steady, and steers his son toward a good apprenticeship.
S4.feel: Uneasy but more hopeful, like opening a new shop.
S4.quote: A father and son business, like my dad and me.
S4.fieldNote: With a decade, Aaron dreams of rebuilding the family business he lost, this time with his son. He is cautious about debt after the shop. His hope is that people will still want a person in their home.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, because both of us would lose work at once, and there's no time to build anything. What would help is proper apprenticeships for adults, and help for small businesses starting out, like cheaper loans. Not benefits, but a chance to work.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about my father. He worked six days a week for forty years, and the shop still closed. I learned you can do everything right and still lose. So I don't believe anyone who says it'll all be fine.

headlineQuote: I learned you can do everything right and still lose.
portrait: Aaron Gupta, 43, runs the edge-bander at a kitchen cabinet factory after closing his father's corner shop when a supermarket moved in. He uses AI now and then once others have proven it, defends a company's right to automate, and asks for apprenticeships rather than handouts. Because his wife's bookkeeping is also exposed, steady change already makes him anxious, and fast AGI brings back the shop's collapse. With five or ten years he plans to rebuild a family business fitting kitchens, ideally with his son.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most, because he and his wife would lose work at the same time with no time to build anything.
whatWouldHelp: Proper apprenticeships for adults and help for small businesses starting out, such as cheaper loans, rather than benefits.
